statement: For cluster owners, the system should maximize cluster utilization while still meeting service commitments.
For cluster owners, the system should protect important workloads.
For cluster owners, the system should keep resource allocation fair and predictable.
For end users, the system should complete batch jobs within budget and by their deadline.
The scheduler should make choices that reflect the tradeoff between what end users are willing to spend and how urgent the work is.
For the existing cluster management system, the system should continue accepting jobs.
For the existing cluster management system, the system should continue handling platform-level control around Libra.
Libra should act as the decision-making layer for scheduling and resource allocation.
The surrounding cluster system should remain responsible for job submission, queueing, and execution plumbing.
Owners should set policy and budget or deadline expectations.
Users should submit their jobs with the constraints set by owners.
Libra should translate user constraints into an actual allocation on the available resources.
Libra should make scheduling decisions based on budget.
Libra should make scheduling decisions based on deadline.
Libra should fit alongside the existing cluster management system.
The system shall schedule jobs fairly for different users.
The system shall help meet user service goals.
The system shall not disrupt the rest of the platform.
Users shall submit batch jobs through the existing cluster management system.
Batch job scheduling shall be based primarily on available resources.
Batch job scheduling shall not be based on user-specific service goals such as budget or deadlines.
Libra shall make the allocation decision before execution.
Libra shall make scheduling more goal-driven.
Libra shall place jobs with the user's budget and deadline in mind instead of using a first-come, first-served approach.
Libra shall choose appropriate execution resources and enforce that allocation so users get predictable outcomes.
Libra shall better align the user's spending limit with the time when the result is needed.
Libra shall handle conflicts between budget and deadline goals.
Libra shall be able to explain, at least at a basic level, why a job was scheduled the way it was.
Notifications and reporting are useful secondary features.
Notifications and reporting should be prioritized only if they are needed for users to understand delays or overruns.
Libra should support rejecting or deferring a job when no viable allocation exists.
Libra must fit cleanly into the existing cluster management flow.
The first version of Libra shall prioritize the core scheduling decision based on budget and deadline.
Libra shall evaluate each submitted job to determine whether it can be run within the user's budget while still meeting the deadline.
If multiple ways exist to run a job within the user's budget and deadline, Libra shall choose the most suitable one based on the job's needs and available cluster resources.
If policy allows it, Libra shall choose the better tradeoff when both the budget and the deadline cannot be satisfied.
The system shall support a tradeoff policy that can vary per user or per job.
The system shall allow deadline to take priority over cost for workloads where meeting the deadline is critical.
The system shall provide a configurable default tradeoff policy.
Libra should consider cost when choosing suitable execution resources.
Libra should respect reservation or queueing constraints in the cluster as part of the resource-selection decision.
Cluster operators shall provide input on the feasibility of Libra requirements.
Cluster operators shall provide input on enforcement requirements for Libra.
Job submitters shall be considered because they care about predictability.
Job submitters shall be considered because they care about pricing.
Job submitters shall be considered because they care about how failures or deferrals are explained.
Finance stakeholders shall be considered because the system is tied to budgets.
Capacity-planning stakeholders shall be considered because the system is tied to utilization.
The system shall support scheduling for a shared cluster.
The system shall consider user job budgets when scheduling jobs.
The system shall consider user job deadlines when scheduling jobs.
The system shall prioritize meeting user budget and deadline goals rather than maximizing raw throughput.
The system shall provide users with predictable service while preventing resource usage from becoming excessive.
The cluster shall support different priority levels fairly.
The platform shall offer flexible service tiers rather than a one-size-fits-all scheduler.
The system shall be evaluated by how often jobs finish by their deadline.
The system shall be evaluated by how much of the cluster is kept busy.
Libra should be conservative about resource commitments.
If scheduling conditions start to drift, Libra should fall back to safer allocations.
The main stakeholders include cluster owners or operators.
The main stakeholders include users or teams submitting jobs.
The platform or infrastructure team that runs the surrounding cluster management system is a stakeholder.
Decision-making usually sits with the operations and platform leads.
Users shall submit jobs with an agreed budget and deadline.
A budget is the amount a user is willing or allowed to spend for a job or workload.
A deadline is the time by which a job is expected to finish.
Priority means how the system should prefer one job over another when resources are tight.
If a budget and a deadline conflict, Libra shall make the best feasible choice rather than violating both.
Libra shall avoid letting one well-funded user monopolize the cluster when other users have acceptable jobs waiting.
Libra shall not receive jobs directly from end users.
Libra shall not directly dispatch jobs to machines.
Libra shall use the job and user information already provided by the platform.
Libra shall enforce the allocation through the same environment in which it operates.
Libra shall minimize disruption to the surrounding system.
The interface between Libra and external systems shall support both reading state and pushing placement or reservation decisions.
Slow or incomplete integrations shall constrain how quickly Libra can reschedule and how confidently it can make commitments.
Budgets and deadlines shall be created when the user submits a job or when the platform attaches the user’s current policy to that submission.
Budgets and deadlines shall remain mostly fixed for a job after creation.
An admin or support path may be provided to correct obvious mistakes or apply an approved change to budgets and deadlines.
Budgets and deadlines shall be validated up front to ensure the values are present and sensible.
When a job finishes or is canceled, its budget and deadline records shall move into normal history or audit storage instead of remaining active in scheduling.
Libra shall favor feasibility first.
Libra shall avoid giving such precedence so often that lower-budget or more flexible users are starved.
Libra shall include some notion of proportional fairness or throttling.
Libra shall balance meeting service commitments with keeping overall cluster use balanced.
The exact balance shall be set by policy rather than left completely to the scheduler.
When budget, deadline, and fairness constraints conflict, deadline commitments should take first priority if the job is still realistically schedulable.
Budget should be treated as the next hard limit.
Libra should not silently exceed the budget unless there is an explicit override or a previously approved policy exception.
Fairness should be treated as a global balancing rule across many jobs rather than as an absolute per-job constraint.
Libra may favor a single urgent job when needed if the system maintains a reasonable overall distribution over time.
If Libra handles customer or employee data, access controls and retention rules should apply.
Access controls and retention rules should influence what Libra stores versus what it only references from the cluster system.
Libra should expose clear status and decision feedback for platform and operations teams rather than a very fancy end-user interface.
Libra should allow platform and operations teams to see why a job was placed, deferred, or rejected.
Libra should show the budget or deadline condition that drove a job placement, deferral, or rejection decision.
Libra should provide controls for overrides or policy tuning when things go wrong.
Libra should support operational clarity and quick troubleshooting so users can trust the scheduler and intervene without digging through logs.
Libra shall be learnable through good operational documentation.
Libra shall provide a short onboarding guide for new team members.
The onboarding guide shall explain the policy model.
The onboarding guide shall explain common scheduling outcomes.
The onboarding guide shall explain how to interpret budget-related rejections.
The onboarding guide shall explain how to interpret deadline-related rejections.
Libra shall provide in-system tooltips as guidance.
Libra shall provide reason codes as guidance.
Libra shall provide example scenarios as guidance.
The system should provide simple visualizations of queue position.
The system should provide simple visualizations of expected start time.
The system should provide simple visualizations of budget consumption.
The system should provide simple visualizations of deadline risk.
The system should support interactive explanations or drill-down views into why a job was delayed.
The interactive explanations or drill-down views should remain lightweight and should not slow down the operational workflow.
The system shall provide explanations in plain language.
The system shall avoid relying only on technical terms or internal policy names in explanations.
The system shall make explanations understandable to people with different backgrounds.
The system shall support screen readers.
The system shall use colorblind-safe visuals.
The system shall provide text alternatives for charts and status indicators.
The system shall allow users to expand explanations into more detail only when needed.
The system shall present decision outputs in a way that both casual users and experienced operators can trust without being overwhelmed.
The system should provide a timeline or Gantt-style chart showing job start and finish expectations.
The system should provide simple queue and utilization indicators for each cluster resource.
The system should provide budget and deadline badges that change color when a job is at risk.
The system should provide a drill-down panel that shows the exact reason a job was placed ahead of another job.
The system should provide an audit trail view that records the input conditions and the policy decision.
Libra shall log enough detail to explain and reproduce a scheduling decision.
Libra shall not necessarily store full job payloads or any sensitive content.
Libra's audit record shall include who submitted the job.
Libra's audit record shall include the relevant budget inputs.
Libra's audit record shall include the relevant deadline inputs.
Libra's audit record shall include the policy version.
Libra's audit record shall include the decision outcome.
Operators shall be able to investigate issues without exposing unnecessary data.
Libra shall retain more detailed records only as long as business needs require.
Libra should be designed to fit common enterprise least-privilege access controls.
If Libra is deployed in a regulated environment, it must be adapted to the company’s legal and compliance team requirements at that time.
Libra shall be scalable when the cluster grows or job arrival rates become bursty.
Libra shall handle higher scheduling throughput without becoming the bottleneck.
Libra shall degrade gracefully if it cannot make every optimal decision instantly.
Libra shall keep its scheduling logic efficient.
Libra shall minimize central state contention.
Libra shall separate fast placement decisions from slower accounting or reporting work.
Capacity needs shall grow with the number of jobs and with the complexity of decision-making as users, policies, and deadlines increase.
The system shall maintain predictable scheduling latency during spikes so jobs do not wait too long for placement.
The system shall account for state size as a capacity planning concern.
Budget tracking, deadline tracking, and policy history shall be considered as state that accumulates over time and affects memory and recovery behavior.
The system should keep the core decision path as stateless as possible.
The system should store shared state in a way that can be partitioned by user, queue, or cluster segment.
The system should avoid updating shared state through one hot central lock.
The scheduler should continue moving even when background accounting is busy.
If the platform allows it, the system should use a sharded or distributed control-plane approach instead of one monolithic scheduler process.
In degraded mode, Libra shall fall back to simpler, faster placement rules instead of trying to compute the best possible allocation every time.
In degraded mode, Libra may use cached decisions.
In degraded mode, Libra may use conservative defaults.
In degraded mode, Libra may use queue-based prioritization so jobs continue to move forward even when some economic optimization is skipped.
Libra shall correct deferred optimization once load drops.
The system shall handle spikes in incoming jobs.
The system shall evaluate larger amounts of state for each scheduling decision.
The system shall manage contention around shared budget or deadline data.
The system shall maintain consistent placement quality.
In degraded mode, Libra shall use earliest deadline first as a straightforward scheduling heuristic.
In degraded mode, Libra shall use oldest job first as a straightforward scheduling heuristic.
In degraded mode, Libra shall use basic budget-aware prioritization to make quick decisions without heavy computation.
Libra shall reserve a small amount of capacity for higher-priority or near-deadline work to avoid starving urgent jobs.
Libra's degraded-mode rules shall be predictable and conservative.
Libra shall keep the cluster making steady progress instead of oscillating between overcommitment and idle resources.
Migration to Libra is a high-risk part of the transition.
The migration must not interrupt normal job submission.
The migration must not lose trust in the existing workflow.
Libra should initially run in parallel with the current scheduling system.
Libra should take over only certain queues or job classes during the initial cutover.
The migration process should allow decisions from Libra and the current scheduling system to be compared before full switching.
The migration must avoid mismatched policies.
The migration must avoid unexpected performance differences.
In-flight jobs must remain consistent during the transition.
The migration process shall include a pilot phase, followed by a limited production phase, and then a broader rollout.
In the pilot phase, Libra shall observe and shadow decisions without controlling execution.
During the pilot phase, platform and operations teams shall compare outcomes and detect policy mismatches early.
If something goes wrong, the system shall support a clean rollback to the existing scheduler with job state preserved.
The transition shall have clear operational ownership so the switch can be made quickly without manual cleanup.
Libra should import user budget balances from the current system.
Libra should import deadline or priority metadata from the current system.
Libra should import the current queue state from the current system.
Libra should import enough cluster capacity information to understand what is already committed.
Libra should import recent job history from the current system.
Data imported into Libra should be consistent and timely.
Libra should use a reliable snapshot of fast-changing data when scheduling to avoid stale or conflicting information.
During migration, the existing system shall remain the source of truth initially, and Libra shall read replicated state rather than directly rewriting it.
The system shall perform reconciliation checks for job status, budget updates, and deadline changes.
The system shall detect any mismatch before a scheduling action is committed.
The system shall use idempotent updates.
Instability under sudden demand spikes shall not affect the whole cluster.
The platform team shall own the job flow integration during each phase of the migration.
The operations team shall monitor cluster health, alerts, and capacity trends during each phase of the migration.
The migration process shall support early problem detection through monitoring of cluster health, alerts, and capacity trends.
During migration, the system shall provide a shared dashboard with live scheduling decisions, queue latency, budget consumption, and node utilization so both teams can view the same signals.
The system shall send alerts to both platform and operations teams when deadline misses are detected.
The system shall send alerts to both platform and operations teams when unusual requeues are detected.
The system shall send alerts to both platform and operations teams when there is a sharp rise in failed placements.
Each migration phase shall have a named on-call owner so escalation is immediate.
Rollback decisions shall be made jointly based on either a predefined threshold or a clear operator judgment call.
Rollback shall be executed through a single switchback procedure that platform can trigger while operations confirms cluster health and monitors recovery.
The system shall include constraints that eliminated other options in decision logs.
The system shall provide exception logs for failed scheduling decisions.
The system shall provide exception logs for overridden scheduling decisions.
The system shall provide periodic summary reports that compare Libra's choices against the old scheduler.
Alerts shall be prioritized first for conditions that threaten job loss or a broad cluster slowdown.
Alerts shall be prioritized after that for localized anomalies or reporting inconsistencies.
The escalation process shall use a bridge call for severe incidents.
The escalation process shall include a handoff path in which platform leads the scheduling logic discussion and operations leads the infrastructure response.
The cluster scheduler shall not use a purely first-come, first-served approach when teams care about business outcomes such as finishing urgent work on time and staying within budget.
The cluster scheduler shall treat a technically runnable job as an unsuitable choice when it would consume too much spend or miss a deadline that matters to a customer or internal delivery.
The cluster scheduler shall account for constrained cluster capacity, including situations where there are more jobs than resources, when deciding which jobs to run.
The cluster scheduler shall account for differing priorities among users and teams when deciding which jobs to run.
The cluster scheduler shall give special consideration to jobs with explicit deadlines, fixed budgets, or high business impact and make tradeoffs instead of maximizing raw throughput.
The scheduler shall satisfy the user’s stated goal for each job.
The scheduler shall use deadline and budget as key signals for satisfying the user’s stated goal.
If both a deadline and a budget are present, the scheduler shall try to meet the deadline without exceeding the budget.
There is no universally defined rule for which of deadline or budget wins in every conflict.
If the deadline and budget goals cannot both be met, the policy must be clarified by the business owners.
The scheduling capability shall sit between the existing job submission path and the actual resource allocation in the cluster.
The surrounding cluster management system shall continue to handle receiving jobs and dispatching them into the workflow.
Libra shall take over when a batch job is submitted and requires a placement or execution decision based on the user's constraints.
Libra's responsibility shall begin when it receives a submitted job with the relevant metadata.
Libra's responsibility shall end after it has selected suitable execution resources and enforced that allocation.
The scheduling capability shall not replace the existing platform's basic job intake.
The scheduling capability shall not replace the existing platform's monitoring function.
The scheduling capability shall not replace the existing platform's infrastructure management functions unless that is later decided otherwise.
The system shall identify cluster owners or operators as main stakeholders.
The system shall identify users who submit jobs as main stakeholders.
The system shall identify the team responsible for the surrounding cluster management platform as a main stakeholder.
The scheduler shall consider users' deadlines when making scheduling decisions.
The scheduler shall consider users' budgets when making scheduling decisions.
The scheduler shall aim to keep the cluster efficient.
The scheduler shall avoid unfair allocations.
The scheduler shall avoid wasteful allocations.
The scheduler shall balance individual job goals against overall cluster health and policy.
Operators shall define any hard constraints or fairness rules.
Libra shall follow operator-defined hard constraints or fairness rules.
Libra shall try to give users the best possible outcome for their submitted jobs.
Users or operators may describe a job using the terms deadline, budget, priority, or urgency.
Users or operators may describe a job's limits using the terms cost cap, spend limit, or must-finish-by time.
Users or operators may describe exceptions using the terms overrides or special handling for critical work.
The vocabulary used to describe scheduling intent and constraints is not fully standardized, and some teams may use their own terms.
Libra shall follow the explicit policy attached to the job or the user when deciding how to handle the job.
Libra shall not guess from urgency alone when deciding how to handle the job.
If the intent is unclear or the constraints conflict, Libra shall be conservative and hold the job or fall back to the default order until someone with authority overrides it.
A single universal tie-breaker has not been defined yet.
In unclear or conflicting cases, Libra shall avoid making an aggressive choice that could violate budget, deadline, or fairness rules.
Submitted jobs are mostly regular batch workloads from the existing platform.
Submitted jobs include compute jobs that can be queued and placed on available resources rather than treated as interactive requests.
The scheduler shall rely on the user or team identity when deciding how to treat a submitted job.
The scheduler shall rely on the budget or cost limit, if one exists, when deciding how to treat a submitted job.
The scheduler shall rely on the deadline or expected completion time when deciding how to treat a submitted job.
The scheduler shall rely on any priority or policy tags attached to the submission when deciding how to treat a submitted job.
If the listed fields are missing, the scheduler shall rely more on default cluster policy and on resource estimates inferred from the job itself.
Libra shall defer a job if it cannot find suitable resources immediately without violating the user's deadline, budget, or any cluster policy.
Libra shall reschedule a job if the environment changes after intake.
Environment changes that can trigger rescheduling include capacity dropping, a higher-priority policy coming in, or the job's predicted cost or runtime moving outside its limits.
Libra shall keep re-evaluating a deferred job until it can place the job safely or until the job becomes impossible under the stated constraints.
If the job becomes impossible under the stated constraints, Libra shall report the failure clearly rather than leaving the job in limbo.
The system shall prioritize execution resources that can meet the job’s deadline.
The system shall prioritize execution resources that can stay within budget.
The system shall consider current load when evaluating execution resources.
The system shall consider estimated runtime on a resource when evaluating execution resources.
The system shall consider policy or reservation rules that make a node unsuitable when evaluating execution resources.
When multiple execution resources are acceptable, the system shall choose the one that best balances cost and completion likelihood.
The system shall check memory before assigning a job.
If the cluster supports it, the system shall check GPU availability before assigning a job.
Libra shall honor affinity, locality, or specialization rules when the job or the platform expresses those rules.
Libra shall use preference-only rules to guide placement without blocking the job entirely.
Deadline and budget shall be treated as the primary hard constraints.
Priority and urgency shall influence ordering and resource choice only after the hard limits are satisfied.
An explicitly stated override in the submission shall take precedence over the default interpretation of priority, urgency, or other terms.
When the relevant terms conflict and the job does not specify which term wins, Libra shall follow the stricter interpretation.
When the relevant terms conflict and the job does not specify which term wins, Libra shall favor the deadline or the lower-cost path rather than assuming the most urgent request should jump ahead.
The job intent vocabulary should be recorded as tentative for now.
The exact meanings and override rules for the intent terms should not be locked down until they are checked with the platform owners and users.
Libra shall mark a job as unschedulable for now when it cannot place the job within the stated constraints.
Libra shall report which constraint blocked scheduling.
Libra shall keep waiting or retrying only when the failure is caused by temporary conditions.
If the platform has a retry policy, Libra should follow that retry policy.
When the margin is too thin, Libra should stop and report that the job is unlikely to succeed rather than waiting until it is already late.
Within the operator policy envelope, the user's budget and deadline shall guide the scheduling choice.
Authority shall shift only if the operator explicitly grants a higher-priority override class.
Emergency jobs and administrative jobs are examples of higher-priority override classes.
The system shall handle periods when many batch jobs arrive at once.
The system shall support high throughput when batch jobs arrive at the start of a business day or after a large data ingest finishes.
The system shall keep the queue moving during high-throughput periods.
The system shall account for uneven job sizes.
The system shall keep the cluster stable.
The system shall avoid overcommitting resources just to clear the queue faster.
Libra shall be designed to work across a range of cluster sizes.
Libra shall be designed to work with relatively small pools and larger shared clusters.
The exact cluster capacity for Libra shall depend on the deployment.
Libra shall not assume a specific cluster size.
If conditions change while a job is running, Libra should try to adjust the allocation plan so the job can continue under the new reality.
Libra's adjustment of the allocation plan must still respect the user's constraints and operator policy.
Libra should prefer controlled rescheduling or rebalancing over abrupt interruption unless operator rules require a preemption or the job can no longer be supported safely.
Libra shall not manage jobs outside the platform to enforce resource allocations.
Libra shall rely on the scheduler and the underlying execution environment to reserve resources according to the plan.
Libra shall rely on the scheduler and the underlying execution environment to assign resources according to the plan.
Libra shall rely on the scheduler and the underlying execution environment to reclaim resources according to the plan when needed.
Libra shall use a cluster-native control that the surrounding platform can actually apply and observe.
The scheduling decision shall be made fast enough that the job remains schedulable before its deadline or before the available budget is wasted waiting.
If the scheduler waits too long, the decision may no longer matter because the job can become infeasible.
The system shall get the first scheduling decision right for short-deadline jobs, jobs with tight budgets, and periods when the cluster is under heavy load.
A bad first scheduling choice can consume the remaining slack and make recovery impossible.
Users shall not be required to submit jobs directly to Libra.
Libra shall fit cleanly into the current management workflow.
The system's applicable external requirements depend on the deployment and the customer.
Some environments may impose data residency, security, or isolation rules that restrict where certain workloads can run.
The platform shall support compliance requirements through policy inputs rather than hardcoding a single mandatory external standard into Libra.
Any rule about workload sensitivity should be treated as a hard constraint if the operator marks it that way.
Libra should support allowed and disallowed placement scopes.
The exact categories and locations for placement constraints should come from policy configuration rather than being fixed in the product.
The system shall provide at least the final placement choice and the main reasons behind it.
The system shall explain whether a scheduling decision was driven by budget, deadline, or a hard policy constraint.
For operators, the system shall indicate whether Libra used a fallback or rejected other options because they violated constraints.
The system shall not be required to produce a full step-by-step decision trace every time.
The system shall provide enough detail to justify the outcome and support troubleshooting when a user thinks the result was unfair or unexpected.
If the policy conflicts with budget or deadline goals, Libra shall make the conflict visible in the result rather than silently optimizing around it.
The scheduling policy should be adjusted when repeated missed deadlines are observed.
The scheduling policy should be adjusted when budget overruns are observed.
The scheduling policy should be adjusted when users receive placements that technically meet the rules but are clearly poor fits for their workloads.
The scheduling policy should be adjusted when the cluster footprint changes.
The scheduling policy should be adjusted when capacity shifts occur.
The scheduling policy should be adjusted when a new tenant with special isolation requirements is introduced.
The scheduling policy should be tuned to reflect a business priority change toward lower cost over speed.
The scheduling policy should be tuned to reflect a business priority change toward speed over lower cost.
The scheduling policy should be revised when users complain about fairness.
The scheduling policy should be revised when users complain about predictability.
The scheduling policy should be revised when users report too much variance in runtime.
Most scheduling changes should be configurable without code changes.
Only operators or customer admins with the right permissions should be able to configure those changes without code changes.
Budget priority should be adjustable.
Deadline priority should be adjustable.
Policy constraints such as allowed placement scopes should be adjustable.
Fairness settings that affect how jobs are ranked should be adjustable.
Preference settings that affect how jobs are ranked should be adjustable.
Thresholds for when Libra should prefer cheaper resources versus faster ones should be tunable.
The system should allow setting a default behavior for submitted jobs that are missing noncritical information.
The system shall capture the complaint itself.
The system shall capture the job’s budget and deadline.
The system shall capture the actual placement and runtime outcome.
The system shall capture whether the user felt the result was slow.
The system shall capture whether the user felt the result was expensive.
The system shall capture whether the user felt the result was inconsistent with similar jobs.
Signals from multiple jobs or users shall carry more weight than a single isolated complaint.
The system shall use these signals for policy tuning rather than individual one-off overrides.
The system shall use these signals to adjust ranking preferences, fairness rules, or thresholds rather than manually rescheduling each job.
The scheduling policy shall be changed when the same kind of complaint recurs across several jobs or comes from multiple users.
The scheduling policy shall be changed when logs show that similar jobs are being treated very differently without a clear policy reason.
The scheduling policy shall be changed when there are consistent misses on runtime predictions.
The scheduling policy shall be changed when there are repeated near-deadline failures.
The scheduling policy shall be changed when there is a noticeable skew against one tenant or workload class.
A single complaint shall usually not be enough to change scheduling behavior unless it exposes a clear bug, a policy violation, or a serious operational issue.
A single complaint shall be treated as one data point unless a repeated pattern is observed before broader adjustments are made.
A scheduler policy review shall be triggered by a new region coming online.
A scheduler policy review shall be triggered by a significant capacity reduction.
A scheduler policy review shall be triggered by hardware with different performance characteristics.
A scheduler policy review shall be triggered by a new tenant that requires strict isolation or placement restrictions.
A scheduler policy review shall be triggered by a major shift in workload mix.
If a rollout has to be rolled back, the system should revert as quickly as practical to the last known good scheduling behavior.
During rollback, jobs already running should usually be left alone unless there is a hard safety or isolation issue.
During rollback, queued jobs should either go back through the prior scheduler logic or remain queued until the prior scheduler logic is restored.
The scheduler policy should be rolled back all at once rather than partially.
The system shall allow a temporary rollback exception only for critical jobs with hard deadlines.
The system shall allow a temporary rollback exception only for critical jobs with customer commitments.
The system shall allow a temporary rollback exception only for critical jobs with safety or availability implications that would be worse if they waited for the full revert.
The system shall require rollback exceptions to be explicitly approved.
The system shall maintain a clear record of why each rollback exception was made and who authorized it.
The system shall not invent a separate long-term path solely for the rollback period.
Rollback exceptions for critical jobs should require sign-off from the on-call cluster operations person.
If the issue is a serious production issue, rollback exceptions should also require sign-off from either the service owner or an incident commander.
If a rollback exception affects a customer commitment or a large tenant, customer-facing approval may also be required.
Rollback exceptions should be measured in hours rather than days.
If a rollback exception is still needed after it expires, it should be treated as a separate operational decision rather than continuing under the rollback exception.
Normally, the primary approver for a rollback exception shall be the on-call operations owner.

If a rollback exception is tied to a specific customer commitment, a regulated workload, or an incident that spans multiple teams, approval shall shift to the incident commander or the relevant service owner.
If a rollback exception involves a security, compliance, or tenant-isolation issue, authority shall move to the person who owns that control area.
The system shall use a short fixed expiry as the default rule for a rollback exception.
The system shall default the approver to the next person in the formal escalation chain when the on-call operations owner and the incident commander/service owner are unavailable.
The system shall usually use the senior operations manager or the designated delegated duty manager as the default approver.
If there is no named delegate, the system shall not invent an ad hoc approver and shall escalate until it reaches someone with explicit authority.
If nobody reachable has the required authority, the system shall make the exception wait unless the situation is truly urgent and safety-critical.
Customer commitment cases shall be treated as high priority.
Customer commitment cases shall not blindly override all other work or rules.
If a customer-facing deadline is at risk, the customer owner or account manager shall be informed right away.
If a customer-facing deadline is at risk, the operations team shall be made aware so it can decide whether to grant an exception or adjust the allocation.
The scheduler shall prefer meeting the commitment when doing so does not cause broader policy violations or starve other critical work.
Customer commitment cases shall be explicitly marked.
Customer commitment cases shall be tracked.
Customer commitment cases shall be reviewed afterward to determine whether the commitment handling was justified.
The review shall determine whether the exception was necessary to meet a legitimate commitment and whether the impact on the rest of the cluster was acceptable.
If the exception displaced other critical work or caused a broader policy violation, it shall be flagged as allowed but not ideal.
Follow-up action may include a corrective note, a policy adjustment, or tighter approval rules next time, depending on impact severity.
The system shall require the first follow-up action after an approved justified exception to be documenting the decision and the reason it was necessary.
The system shall support maintaining a clear audit trail so that the next review has facts instead of memory.
When capacity is tight, the system shall defer nice-to-have optimizations first.
If a lower-priority capability directly protects an important business outcome, the system shall preserve that capability.
The system shall preserve an optimization when it clearly contributes to a near-term commitment or materially reduces user harm.
The system shall keep an extra scheduler capability running if the job is close to missing a user-facing commitment and the extra work could realistically prevent that miss.
The system shall use a simple urgency threshold and a quick estimate of benefit versus delay to decide whether to run an extra scheduler capability.
The system shall place each job on resources that match the job's budget, deadline, and policy constraints.
Logs or test runs shall show the scheduling decision and the selected resource.
Test cases shall demonstrate that different budgets and deadlines produce the expected resource choices.
Any hard requirement that prevents a job from actually starting or finishing correctly shall be treated as a non-negotiable mismatch.
Insufficient CPU or memory shall be treated as a hard failure.
The wrong GPU type shall be treated as a hard failure.
Not enough scratch space shall be treated as a hard failure.
A partition or reservation rule that blocks execution shall be treated as a hard failure.
The system shall be considered successful when a job meets its deadline or budget target after Libra makes the scheduling decision.
Acceptance testing shall use test scenarios with known expected outcomes.
A tighter job shall either be placed on a faster resource or left unscheduled if no compliant option exists.
Libra shall initially choose a valid allocation.
A later move or preemption shall be acceptable if it is within an allowed policy or is recorded as an external platform action outside Libra’s control.
The audit record shall capture the job identity.
